The foundational premise of voluntary motor control lies in feedback mechanisms—specifically, how these systems break down under stress. Intention tremor arises from excessive positive feedback in goal-directed actions, manifesting as oscillatory motion when attempting precise movements. This mirrors a communication system under overload, where feedback loops amplify noise instead of correcting error. Conversely, Parkinsonian tremor emerges from a mismatch between two distinct feedback pathways: one regulating voluntary motion and another maintaining posture. When the former is disrupted, the latter dominates, producing rest tremor. Both phenomena are characterized by mathematical instability—either oscillatory or static—indicating that the underlying control architecture is sensitive to feedback gain. These insights map directly to GSI's Bayesian inference models, where overconfidence in prior beliefs leads to breakdowns, and to GSE’s state-transition logic, where feedback misalignment results in erroneous motor planning or execution.
